title: React Native + Expo: across the JS/native boundary
domain: React Native and Expo JS/native interoperability on Android and iOS
scope: For software engineers. New Architecture, Hermes, Fabric, TurboModules and Expo Modules; Android/iOS call paths, threading, lifecycle, development builds and update compatibility. Conceptual API examples; no pinned SDK version or benchmark claims. Legacy bridge is historical context.

adaptations: Original 10-topic, four-stage curriculum; pastel notebook palette and numbered overview cards; precise editable interface diagrams; no example branding.

topics.title: One app, three layers
topics.takeaway: React Native is a JS application coordinated with a C++ renderer and platform code; Expo supplies a higher-level module and build workflow.

sections.heading: Mental model
sections.body: Your TS/React logic executes in a JS engine, usually Hermes. React Native hosts it inside an Android or iOS app. C++ infrastructure and platform-specific code connect the JS runtime to native APIs and views. Expo is a toolkit and module layer on this architecture, not an additional rendering engine.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body: A camera screen has React state and JSX in JS, a native camera view on Android/iOS, and an Expo or third-party module that exposes camera methods and events to JS. Permission prompts and camera capture live in platform code.

sections.heading: Engineering choice
sections.body: First look for a maintained native library. Write a small module only for the unsupported platform capability. Audit where data is copied and what thread owns it.

sections.heading: Pitfall and next step
sections.body: Do not call every native interaction “the bridge.” Trace a single button press through JS, module or renderer, and platform API; identify what returns synchronously and what returns later.

figures.title: One app, three layers — mechanism
figures.alt: Conceptual layers. The module path is distinct from rendering; all arrows are interface relationships, not guaranteed threads. Nodes: React + TS, Hermes, JSI / RN C++, Android / iOS, Expo Modules.
figures.caption: Conceptual layers. The module path is distinct from rendering; all arrows are interface relationships, not guaranteed threads.

check.question: Where does Hermes run, and does Expo add another JS runtime?
check.answer: Hermes runs the application JavaScript. Expo modules expose native capabilities into that same React Native app; Expo is not a second application JS runtime.

topics.title: What JSI changed
topics.takeaway: JSI allows direct runtime bindings and native object references, but synchronous calls still consume caller time.

sections.heading: Mental model
sections.body: The legacy bridge queued serialized messages between JS and native. In the New Architecture, JSI lets JS interact with C++ host objects through an engine-independent interface. Native module frameworks build typed or declarative APIs above it.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body: A synchronous getCachedValue() may return a small cached scalar. A synchronous readHugeFile() would block the JS caller until I/O finishes; put I/O in an asynchronous function. This is an illustrative design example.

sections.heading: Engineering choice
sections.body: Keep synchronous APIs bounded and predictable. Pass identifiers or handles for large native assets where a library supports them; measure conversion and end-to-end latency rather than guessing from call count.

sections.heading: Pitfall and next step
sections.body: “Zero-copy everywhere” is false: JSI permits native references but APIs can still convert or copy values. Profile the real path and check ownership and lifetime of referenced native data.

figures.title: What JSI changed — mechanism
figures.alt: Two conceptual interop paths; the lower path removes mandatory bridge serialization, not every copy or scheduling cost. Nodes: Legacy JS, Serialized queue, Native, New JS, C++ host object, Native.
figures.caption: Two conceptual interop paths; the lower path removes mandatory bridge serialization, not every copy or scheduling cost.

check.question: Does “no old bridge” mean there is no boundary cost?
check.answer: No. JSI avoids mandatory JSON-style message serialization, yet conversion, allocation, locks, scheduling and native work can still cost time.

topics.title: Fabric: from JSX to pixels
topics.takeaway: Render creates a C++ shadow tree, commit computes layout, and mount changes host views on the UI thread.

sections.heading: Mental model
sections.body: Fabric is the React Native renderer. It builds an immutable C++ shadow tree for host components, calculates layout, diffs the next tree, and mounts host views. Render and commit may be scheduled in several ways; the UI thread owns host view manipulation.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body: Changing a card title creates affected React elements and shadow nodes, then commits layout and applies a host view update. The native control is not rebuilt from scratch for every React render.

sections.heading: Engineering choice
sections.body: Use normal declarative props for view state. A native view is justified when a platform SDK owns a complex surface, such as a map or camera preview. Keep events and props small and well typed.

sections.heading: Pitfall and next step
sections.body: Do not equate React render with immediate on-screen paint. Draw the render → commit → mount phases and inspect a slow frame for JS work, layout, or UI-thread mount cost.

figures.title: Fabric: from JSX to pixels — mechanism
figures.alt: The common rendering path. Scheduling can differ; the final host-view mutation belongs on the UI thread. Nodes: JSX + state, Shadow tree, Commit + Yoga, Mount, Host views.
figures.caption: The common rendering path. Scheduling can differ; the final host-view mutation belongs on the UI thread.

check.question: What thread can actually change an Android View or iOS UIView?
check.answer: The UI/main thread performs the host view mutation during mount.

topics.title: TurboModule: typed service API
topics.takeaway: A typed JS specification and Codegen tie a native service contract to Android and iOS implementations.

sections.heading: Mental model
sections.body: A TurboModule exposes functions and events. A TypeScript or Flow spec describes types, Codegen emits platform glue, and native Android/iOS implementations fulfill that contract. Fabric components handle native views separately.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body: Define getBatteryLevel(): Promise<number> in a typed module spec, implement the platform query separately in Kotlin and Swift/Objective-C++, and handle rejection or missing capability in JS. This is pseudocode for contract shape, not copy-paste setup.

sections.heading: Engineering choice
sections.body: Choose TurboModule when you need RN Codegen contracts or lower-level C++ integration. Keep the exported surface small and versioned; errors and nullability belong in the API design.

sections.heading: Pitfall and next step
sections.body: Generated types do not make platform behavior identical. Test permission denial, lifecycle and device-specific availability on both platforms.

figures.title: TurboModule: typed service API — mechanism
figures.alt: A nonvisual native service contract. Language details and generated glue vary by module implementation. Nodes: TS/Flow spec, Codegen, Android, iOS.
figures.caption: A nonvisual native service contract. Language details and generated glue vary by module implementation.

check.question: Is a TurboModule the path for custom native visual components?
check.answer: Use a native component/Fabric view for visual surfaces; a TurboModule exposes nonvisual native functions and events.

topics.title: Expo Modules: one API, two platforms
topics.takeaway: Expo’s Swift/Kotlin DSL exposes Function, AsyncFunction, events and views over React Native’s low-level primitives.

sections.heading: Mental model
sections.body: Expo Modules API abstracts JSI and related RN primitives. A module definition names the JS-visible surface. Function executes synchronously on the JS runtime thread; AsyncFunction returns a Promise and by default dispatches native work away from that thread.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body: A biometric SDK wrapper could expose isAvailable as a small cached query and authenticateAsync as an asynchronous operation. Swift and Kotlin implement the same JS-facing intent while each platform handles its own permission and result behavior.

sections.heading: Engineering choice
sections.body: Prefer the Expo DSL for a Swift/Kotlin integration when its API fits. Use a TurboModule when the module needs direct C++ access or RN Codegen contracts. Profile before attributing bottlenecks to either framework.

sections.heading: Pitfall and next step
sections.body: AsyncFunction does not mean “runs on the UI thread.” Explicitly choose the main queue for UI work; view-bound async methods have their own main-thread behavior. Define failure and cancellation semantics.

figures.title: Expo Modules: one API, two platforms — mechanism
figures.alt: The same JS interface leads to separately implemented platform behavior; Expo is an abstraction over the RN boundary. Nodes: JS/TS wrapper, Expo Modules API, Swift module, Kotlin module.
figures.caption: The same JS interface leads to separately implemented platform behavior; Expo is an abstraction over the RN boundary.

check.question: When should an Expo module use AsyncFunction instead of Function?
check.answer: For I/O, long work, or work that must be dispatched to another queue; a synchronous Function runs on the JS caller thread.

topics.title: Threads: keep the caller responsive
topics.takeaway: Decide on a queue from the work itself: short sync work on JS, platform UI mutations on main, slow work away from both.

sections.heading: Mental model
sections.body: The JS thread runs application logic and usually render work; the UI thread alone manipulates host views. React Native may schedule some rendering on the UI thread. Expo Function runs on JS; AsyncFunction can dispatch to a native queue, with .runOnQueue(.main) when UI access is required.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body: For a document picker: start platform UI on main, perform file reading away from main, resolve the Promise with a URI and metadata, then update React state on JS. Avoid sending the whole file through a JS value when a URI suffices.

sections.heading: Engineering choice
sections.body: Bound synchronous work, use async for I/O, and isolate native state touched from multiple queues. Keep main-thread sections short and check cancellation when an activity or view goes away.

sections.heading: Pitfall and next step
sections.body: A Promise can still hide blocking native work if its implementation uses the main queue for CPU-heavy processing. Trace queue hops with profiling and measure both JS and UI frames in a release build.

figures.title: Threads: keep the caller responsive — mechanism
figures.alt: Queue ownership for an illustrative operation; the exact dispatch path depends on the module API and implementation. Nodes: JS thread, Worker / native queue, UI/main thread, Promise / event.
figures.caption: Queue ownership for an illustrative operation; the exact dispatch path depends on the module API and implementation.

check.question: Why can a native synchronous method cause a dropped JS frame?
check.answer: It executes on the JS caller thread and prevents JS work from progressing until it returns.

topics.title: Native events need a lifecycle
topics.takeaway: Events are a subscription with cleanup and throughput policy, not an unlimited stream of JS callbacks.

sections.heading: Mental model
sections.body: Native modules can emit events to JS; Expo Modules provide Events, OnStartObserving and OnStopObserving. The native producer may keep working after a screen disappears unless listener and lifecycle cleanup are explicit.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body: A location feed begins when the first listener subscribes, emits compact coordinates at a useful cadence, and stops on the final unsubscribe. When the app backgrounds, decide whether collection should pause based on product requirements and platform rules.

sections.heading: Engineering choice
sections.body: Coalesce high-frequency telemetry, send bounded payloads, and define ordering, missing-event and resubscription behavior. Use native processing when each sample need not reach JS.

sections.heading: Pitfall and next step
sections.body: Sending every sensor sample to React state can overwhelm rendering. Measure event rate and JS frame drops; reduce frequency or aggregate natively when the UI only needs a summary.

figures.title: Native events need a lifecycle — mechanism
figures.alt: Event lifecycle and data flow. Aggregation and event ordering must be designed for the particular producer. Nodes: Native producer, Subscription, Event payload, JS listener, Cleanup.
figures.caption: Event lifecycle and data flow. Aggregation and event ordering must be designed for the particular producer.

check.question: What should happen when the final JS listener is removed?
check.answer: Stop the native observation or release resources if no other owner needs them.

topics.title: The native binary is an API contract
topics.takeaway: A JS update can only use native APIs already compiled into a compatible binary.

sections.heading: Mental model
sections.body: Expo Go contains a fixed native library set. A development build includes your chosen native packages. CNG generates Android and iOS projects from config; config plugins describe persistent changes to native project files. A runtimeVersion links OTA updates to compatible binaries.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body: Adding a native payment SDK changes the binary. Install it, configure its plugin, create and test new Android/iOS development and production builds, then publish JS updates only to the matching runtime.

sections.heading: Engineering choice
sections.body: Treat every native dependency/config change as a release compatibility event. Use a runtimeVersion policy and test a preview build with the same native runtime before rollout.

sections.heading: Pitfall and next step
sections.body: Editing generated AndroidManifest.xml or Info.plist directly in a CNG workflow can be lost on prebuild. Encode changes in config plugins and check generated projects on both platforms.

figures.title: The native binary is an API contract — mechanism
figures.alt: Build-time native surface and update-time JS surface. An OTA update cannot add a new compiled native module. Nodes: App config, Prebuild / compile, Installed binary, OTA update, runtimeVersion.
figures.caption: Build-time native surface and update-time JS surface. An OTA update cannot add a new compiled native module.

check.question: Why does adding a native package require a new app build?
check.answer: Its native implementation is absent from binaries already installed; an OTA JS update cannot compile that code into them.

topics.title: Measure before moving work native
topics.takeaway: Measure JS frames, UI frames, payload size and native work before deciding which boundary to change.

sections.heading: Mental model
sections.body: A slow screen may be caused by JS computation, too many renders, layout, UI-thread work, image decoding or native callback volume. JSI reduces one class of overhead but is not a universal performance fix. Hermes behavior and profiling should be judged in release builds.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body: If a camera overlay stutters, record JS and UI frame behavior, event frequency and payload size. Try lower event cadence or native aggregation first; compare the same device and scenario after each change.

sections.heading: Engineering choice
sections.body: Set a target interaction and trace a real flow. Change one bottleneck at a time; record median and tail latency, dropped frames and memory on representative Android and iOS devices. These are proposed measurements, not claimed results.

sections.heading: Pitfall and next step
sections.body: A microbenchmark for module calls can miss image conversion, native SDK work and React rerender cost. Validate the user-visible result and watch for regressions in startup, battery or memory.

figures.title: Measure before moving work native — mechanism
figures.alt: A measurement loop, not a claim that native code is inherently faster for a particular workload. Nodes: Symptom, Trace, Hypothesis, Change, Re-measure.
figures.caption: A measurement loop, not a claim that native code is inherently faster for a particular workload.

check.question: What evidence would support moving a per-frame calculation to native?
check.answer: A release-build trace showing repeated boundary or JS work hurting the target frame budget, plus an improved end-to-end measurement after a prototype.

topics.title: One JS API, honest platform behavior
topics.takeaway: Share the public contract, then test platform-specific permission, lifecycle, threading and error behavior independently.

sections.heading: Mental model
sections.body: An API can present the same JS method name on both platforms while Android Activity lifecycle and iOS app lifecycle hooks differ. A good abstraction states common behavior and surfaces capability differences explicitly.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body: For a secure-document scan wrapper, define a discriminated result for success, user cancellation, denied permission and unsupported capability. Implement dismissal/cleanup separately for Android and iOS, then test each path on devices.

sections.heading: Engineering choice
sections.body: Keep the TS facade stable; make platform-specific native tests and contract tests for returned shapes. Version the binary and JS API together when native behavior changes.

sections.heading: Pitfall and next step
sections.body: A simulator success can hide hardware permission and lifecycle problems. Add device checks for background/foreground, rotation or activity recreation where relevant, and app termination.

figures.title: One JS API, honest platform behavior — mechanism
figures.alt: The public API can be shared; platform lifecycle and capability checks remain separate. Nodes: JS contract, Android path, iOS path, Shared tests, Device checks.
figures.caption: The public API can be shared; platform lifecycle and capability checks remain separate.

check.question: Does the same method name guarantee identical Android and iOS semantics?
check.answer: No. Native capabilities and lifecycles differ; the wrapper should document differences and normalize only what can be normalized honestly.
